lessons.title: Mains electricity, plugs and safety
lessons.summary: Find out how mains electricity differs from a battery, what the three wires in a plug do, and why the earth wire and fuse keep you safe.
objectives: I can explain the difference between direct current and alternating current.
I can state the frequency and potential difference of UK mains electricity.
I can describe the colour, potential and job of the live, neutral and earth wires.
I can explain why touching the live wire is dangerous even when a device is switched off.
I can explain how the earth wire and fuse protect a user and an appliance.

activities.title: Direct and alternating current
activities.content:
## Two kinds of current

A cell or battery produces **direct current (d.c.)**. The potential difference stays at a fixed value and the current always flows in the **same direction** round the circuit. On an oscilloscope, a d.c. supply shows as a flat, horizontal line.

The mains supply in your home produces **alternating current (a.c.)**. The potential difference **constantly changes direction**, swinging from positive to negative and back again many times a second. The current therefore flows backwards and forwards. On an oscilloscope, a.c. looks like a wave.

**UK mains electricity**
- Potential difference: about **230 V**
- Frequency: **50 Hz** (the p.d. completes 50 full cycles every second)

Why use a.c. for the mains? It is easy to change the p.d. of an alternating supply using transformers, which lets electricity be transmitted efficiently across the country. Most portable devices use d.c. from batteries, and mains chargers convert a.c. to d.c. for them.

The number of cycles per second is the **frequency**, measured in hertz (Hz). The time for one cycle is the **period**, which for the UK mains is $1/50 = 0.02$ s.

question.text: Which of these correctly describes UK mains electricity?
question.hint: Remember the two numbers: one is a voltage, the other is a frequency.
question.explanation: UK mains is alternating current at about 230 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.

activities.title: Inside a three-pin plug
activities.content:
## The three wires

Most UK appliances connect to the mains through a three-pin plug containing three wires. Each has a job and a colour code you must learn.

| Wire | Colour | Potential | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Live** | Brown | About **230 V** (alternating) | Carries the alternating p.d. from the supply |
| **Neutral** | Blue | **0 V** (or close to it) | Completes the circuit; carries current away |
| **Earth** | Green and yellow stripes | **0 V** | Safety wire; only carries current if there is a fault |

The potential difference between the live wire and the neutral wire (or earth) is about 230 V. This is what drives the current through the appliance.

**Other parts of the plug**
- The **fuse** sits in the live wire, next to the live pin.
- The **cable grip** holds the cable so that the wires cannot be pulled out of their pins.
- The **casing** is made of plastic, an **insulator**, so you cannot touch anything live.
- The **pins** are brass, a good **conductor** that does not corrode easily.

A useful memory aid for colours: **bl**ue is **l**eft... no, better: **BR**own is **R**ight (as you look at the open plug with the cable at the bottom), and the striped earth goes to the top.

activities.title: Worked example: describing a fault
activities.content:
**A student notices that the brown wire in a plug has come loose from its pin and is touching the metal casing of a kettle. Explain the danger.**

1. The brown wire is the **live** wire, so it is at about **230 V**.
2. If it touches the metal casing, the casing also becomes live.
3. A person touching the kettle is at 0 V (earth potential), so there is a p.d. of about 230 V between the casing and the person.
4. A current would flow **through the person to earth**, causing a dangerous electric shock.

**How is this normally prevented?** The metal casing is connected to the **earth wire**. If the live wire touches the casing, a large current flows to earth through the earth wire, the **fuse melts**, and the circuit is broken before anyone is hurt.

Notice the logic used: identify the p.d., identify the path for current, then explain the effect.

question.text: Match each wire in a three-pin plug to its colour.
question.explanation: Live is brown, neutral is blue, earth is green and yellow striped.

activities.title: Why the live wire is dangerous
activities.content:
## Potential difference and shocks

Your body is at roughly the same potential as the ground: **0 V**. The live wire alternates around **230 V**. If you touch the live wire, there is a potential difference of about 230 V between the wire and your body, so a **current flows through you to the earth**.

Even a small current through the heart can be fatal, and the resistance of the human body is low enough, especially with damp skin, for a dangerous current to flow at 230 V.

**Switched off is not the same as safe**

Many students think that an appliance that is switched off must be safe to touch inside. That is wrong. A switch usually only breaks the circuit at one point. If the live wire is still connected to the supply, it is still at 230 V. Touching it will still give a shock, because the current can flow through you to earth instead of through the appliance. The only safe option is to **unplug** the appliance before opening it.

**The neutral wire** is at about 0 V, so the p.d. between it and you is close to zero and it is normally not dangerous. But never rely on that: wiring faults can swap the wires.

question.text: True or false: if a lamp is switched off, it is safe to touch the live wire inside it as long as it is still plugged in.
question.hint: What is the potential of the live wire when the appliance is plugged in but switched off?
question.explanation: False. The live wire is still at about 230 V whenever the appliance is connected to the mains. A p.d. of 230 V between you and the wire will drive a current through your body to earth.

activities.title: Fuses, earthing and double insulation
activities.content:
## Safety devices

**The fuse**
A fuse is a thin piece of wire inside a small cartridge that is connected in the **live** wire. If the current becomes too large, the fuse wire **heats up and melts**, breaking the circuit. This protects the appliance and the wiring from overheating and catching fire.

Choose a fuse rating just **above the normal current** of the appliance. Common ratings are 3 A, 5 A and 13 A. A fuse that is too big would let a dangerous current flow; one that is too small would melt during normal use.

**The earth wire**
Appliances with a metal casing are connected to the earth wire. If a fault makes the casing live:
1. A large current flows from the live wire through the casing and down the earth wire.
2. The large current **melts the fuse**.
3. The appliance is disconnected from the live wire, so the casing is safe again.

The earth wire and fuse work **together**: the earth provides the low-resistance path, and the fuse does the cutting off.

**Double insulation**
Some appliances, such as hairdryers and phone chargers, have a plastic casing and no metal parts you can touch. They are **double insulated** and do not need an earth wire, so their cable has only two wires.

**Circuit breakers** do the same job as fuses but can be reset instead of replaced, and they act more quickly.

activities.title: Worked example: choosing a fuse
activities.content:
**A hairdryer is rated at 230 V, 1800 W. Which fuse (3 A, 5 A or 13 A) should be fitted?**

The normal operating current is found from $P = VI$, so $I = P / V$:

$I = \dfrac{1800}{230} = 7.8$ A

The fuse must be **just above** the normal current, so it does not melt in ordinary use but does melt if a fault makes the current much larger. 3 A and 5 A are too small: they would blow every time the hairdryer was switched on. So the correct choice is the **13 A** fuse.

**A desk lamp is rated at 230 V, 40 W.**

$I = \dfrac{40}{230} = 0.17$ A, so a **3 A** fuse is appropriate.

The power equation $P = VI$ comes from the next sub-topic, but examiners often combine it with plug questions, so it is worth being ready.

question.text: A toaster is rated at 230 V, 920 W. Calculate the normal operating current of the toaster. Give your answer in amps.
question.explanation: I = 920 ÷ 230 = 4 A. A 5 A fuse would be suitable.

question.text: A fault causes the live wire inside a metal-cased heater to touch the casing. Put the events in the order they happen.
question.hint: The earth wire acts first; the fuse acts second.
question.explanation: The casing becomes live, a large current flows through the earth wire, the fuse heats and melts, and the heater is disconnected from the live supply.
order: A large current flows from the casing along the earth wire
The fuse wire heats up and melts
The heater is cut off from the live wire and the casing is safe

question.text:
A washing machine has a metal casing and is connected to the mains using a three-core cable.

(a) State the potential of the live wire and of the earth wire. (2 marks)

(b) Explain how the earth wire and the fuse together protect a person if the live wire touches the metal casing. (3 marks)
question.hint: Think of the earth wire as a path and the fuse as the switch that cuts things off.
question.explanation: (a) Live is about 230 V; earth is 0 V. (b) If the live wire touches the casing, a large current flows through the low-resistance earth wire to the ground. This large current melts the fuse, which breaks the circuit and disconnects the live wire, so the casing is no longer live and nobody can get a shock.

markScheme.criterion: Live wire is at about 230 V
A large current flows through the earth wire (to the ground)
The circuit is broken so the appliance is disconnected from the live supply and the casing is safe

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **d.c.** (cells, batteries): constant direction. **a.c.** (mains): direction keeps reversing.
- UK mains: **230 V, 50 Hz**.
- **Live** = brown, 230 V. **Neutral** = blue, 0 V. **Earth** = green/yellow stripes, 0 V, safety only.
- The live wire is dangerous **even when switched off**, because a p.d. of 230 V exists between it and you (at earth potential).
- **Earth wire + fuse**: a fault makes the casing live, a big current flows to earth, the fuse melts and disconnects the appliance.
- Fuse rating: just above the normal current, found from $I = P/V$.
- Double-insulated appliances have plastic cases and need no earth wire.

practiceQuestions.text: State the frequency of the UK mains supply in hertz.
practiceQuestions.hint: It is the number of cycles per second.
practiceQuestions.explanation: UK mains has a frequency of 50 Hz.

practiceQuestions.text: Which wire in a plug is coloured blue?
practiceQuestions.hint: It is the one that is normally at about 0 V and completes the circuit.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The neutral wire is blue. Brown is live and green/yellow is earth.

metadata.blanksText: The live wire carries an alternating potential of about ___ volts. The neutral wire is at about ___ volts. The fuse is always connected in the ___ wire.

practiceQuestions.hint: The fuse must cut off the dangerous wire.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Live is about 230 V, neutral is about 0 V, and the fuse is in the live wire so that when it melts the appliance is disconnected from the high potential.

practiceQuestions.text: Calculate the time period of one cycle of the UK mains supply. Give your answer in seconds.
An electric iron is rated 230 V, 2300 W. Calculate its normal operating current and state which fuse (3 A, 5 A or 13 A) should be used.
practiceQuestions.hint: I = P ÷ V, then pick the fuse just above that current.
practiceQuestions.explanation: I = 2300 ÷ 230 = 10 A, so a 13 A fuse is needed.

practiceQuestions.text: Which TWO statements about a.c. and d.c. are correct?
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about direction of current and where each type comes from.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A battery gives d.c. in one direction. Mains a.c. keeps changing direction. Both types can drive a current, and both can transfer energy.

options.text: A battery supplies direct current, which flows in one direction only
The mains supplies alternating current, which repeatedly changes direction
Alternating current cannot transfer energy to a heater
Direct current changes direction 50 times a second

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a double-insulated appliance with a plastic casing does not need an earth wire.
practiceQuestions.hint: What is the earth wire connected to in an ordinary appliance?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. There is no exposed metal that could become live, so the earth wire is not needed.

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why a person who touches the live wire of a plugged-in appliance receives an electric shock.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the potential of the wire with the potential of the person.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The live wire is at about 230 V while the person is at 0 V (earth potential). This p.d. drives a current through the person's body to the earth.

markScheme.criterion: There is a potential difference (about 230 V) between the live wire and the person / the earth
A current flows through the person (to earth)

practiceQuestions.text: A student fits a 13 A fuse in the plug of a lamp that normally draws 0.2 A. Explain why this is a poor choice.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does a fuse need to do if a fault occurs, and what current would be needed to melt this one?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A fuse should be rated just above the normal current. A 13 A fuse would allow a fault current far larger than 0.2 A to flow without melting, so the lamp and its wiring could overheat or catch fire before the fuse blew.

markScheme.criterion: Fuse rating should be just above the normal current (e.g. 3 A)
A dangerously large fault current could flow without the fuse melting, so the appliance could overheat / catch fire

practiceQuestions.text:
A kettle with a metal body is rated at 230 V, 3000 W.

(a) Calculate the current in the kettle when it is working normally. (2 marks)

(b) Explain why the kettle's plug contains a fuse and its cable contains an earth wire. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: I = P ÷ V. Then think about what each safety feature protects against.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) I = 3000 ÷ 230 = 13 A (13.0 A). (b) The fuse melts if the current gets too large, protecting the wiring from overheating. The earth wire is connected to the metal body: if the live wire touches it, a large current flows to earth and blows the fuse so the body cannot give a shock.

markScheme.criterion: Fuse melts if current is too large, protecting against overheating / fire
Earth wire gives a path so the metal casing cannot stay live / prevents a shock
